DR. K. R. EISSLER IS THE SECRETARY of the Sigmund Freud Archives, Inc., which has deposited a large collection in the Library of Congress. The 1951 agreement was one which the Library of Congress should not, I think, have undertaken; for they did not anticipate that despite the restrictions on access to others, Dr. Eissler has made copies of material, felt free to send these around (for instance to Ernest Jones), and cited what he chooses in behalf of his effort to idealize Freud. A Joint Committee on Archives, which both the American Historical Association and the Society of Archivists support, is making continuing inquiries into the status of the Sigmund Freud Collection in Washington.

In 1971 Dr. Eissler initiated his assault on my Brother Animal: The Story of Freud and Tausk(1969), and in so doing cited details from an unpublished letter Freud wrote in 1934. Dr. Eissler then put the following footnote: "The letter is contained in the collection of the Sigmund Freud Archives. It is the Archives' policy not to make its collection accessible, for the time being, to the public. The Board of Directors has given me special permission to deviate in this instance from this policy." (Eissler, 1971) Later, after my article (1972) of rebuttal, "Reflections on ethos and authenticity in psychoanalysis, " challenged Dr. Eissler's use of archival material, he wrote in connection with his reliance on that 1934 unpublished letter:

In my quotation from this document, which is contained in the collection of the Sigmund Freud Archives, the same facts that are known from other sources are presented. The Board of the Archives thought, I think rightly, that under these circumstances the exception is not a breach of the general rule that governs the administration of the Archives. This is the only instance where I have made use of a document from the Archives' collection. (Eissler, 1974)

Dr. Eissler does not state why, if "the same facts" were indeed available elsewhere, he chose to rely on the Sigmund Freud Archives. It is not true that that was the "only instance" where he made use of a document from the collection.

THE CAREFUL AND THOUGHTFUL DISCUSSIONS of Drs. Crowley and Davis, with added insights and examples, make any further additions on my part about Sullivan's view of personal individuality unnecessary. However, I feel I must make some reply to the comments of Drs. Lionells and Lefer, limiting myself, however, to the still unresolved issue of unique self or individuality. (To reply to all their comments and objections would require more space and excursions afield from the main issue than this reply warrants.)

Dr. Lionells uses an argument that is weak on both logical and psychological grounds when she writes that the idea of unique self is "a defense against the terrible anxiety produced by ones inability to attain intimacy." The validity of a statement has little to do with the person who asserts it or indeed the reason why he or she asserts it. In any case Dr. Lionells must know that anything and everything can be used defensively. This includes "consensual validation, " e.g. "I must be feeling this way because everyone does under these circumstances;" or, "I acted according to orders, " within the consensual framework. People of the 20th century may suffer from alienation but they suffer at least as much from the group pressures of a mass society, the pressures of enforced "togetherness" or worse. What puzzles me about Dr. Lionells' paper is that while I agree with her that one of the tasks of the analyst is to help the individual attain the possibility of intimacy (should the patient so desire), I still do not understand how this conflicts with the idea of personal individuality.

Dr. Lefer seems to be stating that unique individuality is the same as alienation, the latter defined in terms of interpersonal theory. He is essentially asserting that one has creative thoughts, original and unconventional life styles and so on because one has no alternative way of "seeking security and satisfaction, " and not because of, for example, pleasure or particular values. Alienation, according to Webster, means "estrangement from." One can be estranged from self as well as estranged from others.

FREUD WAS ABLE TO SAY THAT "our metapsychology is a mythology" Like Athena coming full grown out of Zeus' forehead, Freud's metapsychology also erupted from his creative use of clinical experience. However, he realized that what he had to say after leaping from observable neurological phenomena to psychoanalytic theory was difficult to prove. Thus did "mythology" become the foundation of a psychoanalytic theory.

Sullivan did not want a mythology. The importance of participant observation required setting limits to theory building. Also, he did not wish to build a theory that claimed to explain all human psychology, since that would be presumptuous and beyond the realm of any one person. What is observable, workable, and part of experience that can be consensually validated was the aim of interpersonal hypotheses. He was able to leave a foundation that can grow, change, develop, rather than stopping at a "mythology" where all is walled-in, and any new development in theory interchanged with a static language.

Dr. Klenbort's paper is an attempt to take on Sullivan's ideas concerning the "illusion of personal individuality". She calls his concepts an "intellectual ambivalence". Since ambivalence is a feeling state, I find this difficult to grasp. Ideas change as Sullivan changed. This is seen in his later ideas when they are contrasted with those of his Personal Psychopathology.

Maurice Green  

IT IS FITTING IN THIS twentieth anniversary year of the death of Clara M. Thompson to recognize and pay homage to her pioneering work in psychoanalysis and to her long lasting friendship and collaboration with Harry Stack Sullivan. Her paper, Sullivan and Psychoanalysis, deserves its reprinting here.1 Sullivan was, uniquely, her mentor, and for a short time, her patient. They met about 1925 when she was a protege of the eminent Adolf Meyer. Clara, in her typical New England conscientiousness, was working hard presenting a patient at a staff conference to which the famous Sullivan had been invited to attend. She had a fever of 103°F and Sullivan was immediately attracted to her.

At that time Meyer (who had preserved the American Psychoanalytic Association from being dissolved by William Alanson White in 1919) had become embittered over the political attempts of Freud and his group in Vienna to dominate and control psychoanalysis in America. When Meyer found out that Clara was seeking psychoanalytic treatment he dismissed her from his service. However, she found great comfort and encouragement in Sullivan, who supported her efforts to become independent and seek psychoanalytic training in Budapest. Sullivan had already vainly tried to have Ferenczi brought to Washington, but William Alanson White adamantly refused, implying that such visitors were mainly after money. So in 1928 he was helpful to her in her decision to go to Budapest and study with Sandor Ferenczi, with the understanding that she in turn would analyze Sullivan, so the story goes.

To the Editor:

WESTERN PSYCHIATRIC LITERATURE assumes that psychiatry in the Socialist countries is basically organically oriented. A similar view pervades in Israel, and that view is reinforced by contacts with some of the new immigrants from those countries. Therefore, it came to me as a surprise to learn from the journal Psychoterapia1 that two symposia had been held on the topic of psychotherapy, the first in March, 1973 in Prague, Czechoslovakia, and the second, in Komorov (near Warsaw) Poland, at the end of May, 1976. Representatives from Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland and the USSR participated.

All the participants stressed the importance of the role of psychotherapy in the treatment of various disturbances. Statistically, the need for psychotherapy was found in at least 25% of all patients, of whom it was thought 60% could be treated psychotherapeutically by general practitioners who would require special training. In addition to the need to develop methods for short-term psychotherapy, there was concern expressed with the formulation of criteria as to which patients qualified for such treatment. Of particular interest was the emphasis on the need to train medical students in the fields of psychology and psychopathology and the basic elements of psychotherapy. It was thought that general practitioners should be trained in diagnosing functional disturbances in which psychogenic factors play a primary role.

Readers are invited to send in brief commentaries or critical evaluations of issues raised in this Journal or in the psychoanalytic field in general. These communications should be no more than five pages, and should be addressed to the Editor.

SULLIVAN'S PROPOSAL FOR A TRANFORMATION of a felt "need for tender cooperation" to an enactment of malevolent behavior toward the very person from whom tenderness is desired runs something as follows: By virtue of prolonged repetitive experience in being rebuffed when tenderness was solicited, one eventually takes it for granted that all such future overtures will be met by similar rebuffs. Wishing, reasonably, to cut his losses such a person attempts to foreclose future rebuff by attacking pre-emptively, rejecting before being rejected, preserving thereby some small measure of pride at the cost of virtually guaranteeing rejection itself. As Sullivan puts it, "he beats them to it, " engendering "the attitude that one really lives among enemies."1

We know these people at their most blatant by the hostile winds which they push before themselves, by the chronic chip on the shoulder, by the itching for a fight, at their most subtle by their chronic contempt veiled as cynicism, sarcasm, hauteur, derogation. In their younger days they were the meanest kids on the block, specialists in bullying and vandalism. It is indeed an old story which must include all the spoilers in history, from Cain to the humorous variations on "Keep your damn lawn mower!"

The ubiquity of this turn toward malevolence, in all its variations, is beyond question. There are, however, two aspects of Sullivan's formulation which I find not fully satisfying as an account of the strong cases of malevolence. IN DYADIC PSYCHOTHERAPY THE PATIENT must test the safety of the relationship with the therapist gradually. Increasing involvement and regression is accompanied by feelings of vulnerability and assaults on self-esteem. As the patient allows himself more latitude in regressive free association, he comes to feel more comfortable about what he perceives as the therapist's opinions and judgments about him. The patient in group therapy is even more open to assaults upon his sense of himself. Fears about what others in the group will think of him are often the strongest deterrent to joining a therapeutic group. There are more people to be trusted with one's weaknesses and secrets. The other patients in the group are not even professionals trained to help others but as psychiatric patients ought not to be trusted. The group is regarded as a "public" forum whereas dyadic therapy is regarded as "private."1 The group situation seems to present a requirement for greater public displays of oneself and at the same time presents greater possibilities of injury to self-esteem than the dyadic situation.

The purpose of this paper is to discuss various facets of the regulation of self-esteem in group therapy. To what extent can the patient's self-esteem be protected by the therapist in the face of the complex and continued threats to it posed by the group? What methods can be used for this kind of protection? What is the optimal balance of exposure and protection in the group?

Gerard Chrzanowski  

To the Editor:

I READ DR. EPSTEIN'S PAPER and Dr. Feiner's discussion (This Journal, Volume 13, 4, October 1977) of it with pleasure. The topic is clinically significant and deserves to be aired in some detail. There are a number of important issues involved. My direct response to the presentation and the reply centers on two aspects only.

1. Dr. Feiner correctly raises the issue of a distinction between feeling tone and action i.e., hatred as an emotion versus destructiveness as a behavioral act. As analysts we also look at the phenomenon of hatred as a potential mask of malevolence, particularly in a "motherless child." Hatred as an emotional manifestation may cover a wide range of pre-occupations. We may find an element of malignity that is a deep-seated and virulent disposition to injure; or rancor which refers to a lasting corrosive resentment; or a complete suit of facial and postural armor as an overlay for basically not feeling acceptable.

Be that as it may, I am surprised that neither Dr. Epstein nor Dr. Feiner make reference to Sullivan's construct of malevolent transformation. In essence the theorem pertains to the substitution of malevolent behavior when a genuine need for tenderness arises. According to Sullivan, malevolence manifests itself when a child's overt need for tenderness leads to increasing frustration and distress in the face of an absence or outright negative environmental response. Sullivan considers the development of malevolence in the formation of personality a profound handicap to the most profitable experience one would have had in subsequent stages of development since "one never feels exceedingly good or worthy."

A systematic, compassionate exploration of the patient's need for tenderness, and her defenses against it, may have distinct merit in the case Dr. Epstein presents.

CHRISTOPHER LASCH WARNS US of the tyranny of our contemporary super state which invades and controls the most private recesses of the human soul through its commercial and therapeutic instruments. The earlier authority of the church and parents has now been displaced by television, corporations, government and various professional groups. Family life has become painful, marriages more fragile and relations between parents and children increasingly filled with hostility and recrimination. In his introduction Lasch repeats again and again that there is no haven in this heartless world.

He sets forth a historical perspective affirming the acculturating instrumentality of the family as an institution for embedding specific culture in specific individuals. He describes the Protestant personality demanded by a capitalist economic order and the increasing importance given to child rearing in the bourgeous family. This family, already beginning to decay as an institution at the end of the 19th century was characterized by a marriage of companionship, child-centered home, the quasi-emancipation of all women, and the isolation of this family from kin and from community. Exclusive sexual fidelity between spouses was abandoned, the virginity standard set aside and martial harmony was suspect with an emphasis on "healthy" marital quarrels. Romantic love was dismissed as "sick" and the orgasm elevated to an inalienable right.

Gilman prophetically declared in 1903 that children were citizens with rights to be guaranteed only by the state, and that those children could no longer be the property of personal ownership.

ONE OF THE QUESTIONS POSED to the panel was "how do your various theories of the self affect your analytic work as it concerns persons presenting characterological, neurotic and borderline problems?"

G. Medini  

PERHARS THE MOST PERVASIVE and longest living theory of truth has to do with a correspondence between a "true" belief and a "fact". Every true belief, and no false belief, corresponds to such a fact. The property common to all truths is such a correspondence. Most commonly associated with this theory is G. E. Moore (1959), although its history stretches back to Aristotle. Ignoring the semantics of "belief" (something may be true though noone believes it), the essential point is that something is true if it corresponds to a fact and false if it does not. Because of the tendency of this approach to lend itself to an all or nothing position, and its obliviousness to the context within which statements are embedded, and because of the difficulty in defining what is and what is not "fact", we can only talk of partial truths. Thus Carnap (1959) emphasizes the element of choice in describing phenomena, in the name of consistency, and with the aim of maintaining a useful symbolic system.

Under closer examination a "correspondence" of statements with facts tends to become less and less clear. To Carnap, then, truth has to do more with maintenance of system consistency. William James (1929) thought the essence of truth has to do with moral choice; beliefs are true to the extent that we act upon them and believe in them. To James, that which acts as constriction of imagination and creative action is, per se, a subtraction of an element from "truth".

There are the semanticists who feel that truth has "meaning" only within a context of specific language. Statements made in one language may lose specific "meaning" or the quality of "truth" if made in another language.

Arthur Feiner  

EDGAR A. LEVENSON has been having a romance with psychoanalytic concepts and concepts about psychoanalysis for the past twenty years. Like watching Fred Astaire in those old movies, deeply in love with his partners, gliding them across chandeliered dance floors, one gets vicarious pleasure observing Dr. Levenson play with analytic ideas. But in the movies of that other generation, I never thought those partners were adequate to Astaire's perfectionism. Reading Dr. Levenson, I get the same feeling. Perhaps that is his essential appeal. His is a fine sensibility.

The systems concept1 has had a long respectable history. Without the term "system" occurring, the idea appears as "natural philosophy" to Leibniz, and to Nicholas of Cusa; as the "coincidence of opposites" to Paracelsus; to Vico's vision of history as a sequence of "cultural entities, " and to the dialectics of Hegel, Marx, and Engels. Even Kohler's "physical gestalten" pointed in this direction. And "holism" was a hallmark in the writings of Kurt Goldstein. There are, of course, theory systems and they are not General Systems Theory. Vico, Hegel, Marx, Spengler, Toynbee, and others, all have systems with which to construct theoretical history. While the differences among these systems are evident, they all agree that the historical process is not accidental but follows ascertainable laws.

A system is defined as a complex of elements in mutual interaction. It is true systems can be classified as closed or open, and while some authors have stated, or implied, that certain theories of psychology and personality are based on the conception of closed systems, Allport, in contradistinction to what Dr. Levenson writes, was evidently of the opinion that we had better leave closed systems to the realm of physics. And even here, referring to Einstein's theory for the transformation of matter into energy, Allport questioned whether this did not demonstrate the futility of positing a closed system even in physics.

ON PAGE 426 OF THIS JOURNAL'S 1977 volume, the reader will find my second request to Professor Roazen for a meeting at which we could attempt to resolve a controversy which has arisen between us concerning certain aspects of Freud's life. In reading Professor Roazen's book Brother Animal, I had found many basic errors of fact which I discussed in Talent and Genius. However, Professor Roazen evidently saw no reason to change his views in any way. Therefore, I thought that a personal meeting might provide the most effective means of clarifying where the errors lie, since our disagreement concerned documented facts.

This second suggestion for a meeting also remained unanswered. In the following essay I shall summarize some instances which, in my opinion, prove beyond any doubt that Professor Roazen has been in error.

In his book Brother Animal(1969), Professor Roazen has given his version of the events that led to Victor Tausk's (1879-1919) suicide. Tausk was an eminently gifted pupil of Freud. He joined the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society in 1911. In 1918 he asked Freud to take him into psychoanalytic treatment. Freud refused and sent him to Helene Deutsch, who at that time was undergoing a training analysis with Freud. After three months she discontinued Tausk's analysis because it became incompatible with her own analysis. In July Tausk committed suicide.

Professor Roazen's book was well received by most reviewers and readers. Its convincing character was based on a few relevant, apparently fully documented, incidents. I shall examine in this essay Professor Roazen's documentation, disregarding the wealth of undocumented "missing links" with which his book is replete.

DR. GERARD CHRZANOWSKI presents a much more clinical survey of Sullivan's ideas, (innovative and incompletely developed as they were), then previous authors (e.g., Green, 1972), . His book lacks the precision of Leston Haven's work which spells out the (albeit limited but nonetheless uniquely valuable) instrumental technique of participant-observation as practiced by Sullivan, and reported in actual cases of Sullivan himself or others whom he closely supervised. However, Dr. Chrzanowski is not so interested in the appreciation of Sullivan's special contribution as he is in appraising the deficiencies and limitations of that contribution; and adding his own modifications, elaborations and present-day research to present Chrzanowski's own theoretical system and clinical practice. This, of course, is a timely and most useful contribution, and high-lights the tragic failure of so many others trained in the Washington School and the White Institute to systematically elaborate the special contributions of Sullivan that have been so influential here and abroad, and to which they are in tremendous debt.

Thus, this short book is appropriately subtitled A Contemporary View of Harry Stack Sullivan and is divided in two parts—the first stating the basic structure and terms of Sullivan's loose, unsystematized theory; and the second describing Chrzanowski's own elaboration in the therapeutic process and its vicissitudes. At the end is included the complete bibliography compiled by Ralph Crowley.

The preface credits Chrzanowski's own and Sullivan's delineation of an interpersonal Self to the pioneering work of Baldwin, Mead and Kurt Lewin. Here Chrzanowski demonstrates the depth psychology of the interpersonal Self in an ecologic frame of reference integrating advanced contemporary research into the interpersonal approach.

WHILE CROSSING THE ATLANTIC last Tuesday I asked myself exactly how I was to express what I wanted to discuss this afternoon. Oral character that I am, I was not surprised to be suddenly reminded of a favorite dessert of mine created in my country of origin, which I had just revisited. It is called Kaiserschmarn, translated as best I can as "The Emperor's Nothing." Legend says that it came into being one fine night when old Kaiser Franz-Joseph woke up famished, summoned his chef, and demanded to be fed. The chef was desperate, for the larder was quite empty. He started throwing together some odds and ends he had around the kitchen, including a lot of sweets and fruits, frantically trying to concoct an omelette. But when he tasted it, he did not deem it fit to be served to a monarch. It seemed too simple. So he tore it into shreds, trying to make it truly a "nothing." The Emperor, however, was not to be deterred, insisted that he was very hungry, ate all of it—and liked it. To this day this "nothing" dessert exists. Well, you are the Emperor, I am the poor chef. Here is my "nothing" omelette, and I do hope you will find it somewhat palatable.

Obviously there are disadvantages and advantages to being the last speaker on a panel like this one. The disadvantage is clearly given by the likelihood—as, indeed, proved to be case today—that preceding commentators have said all that is worth saying on the topic. Ah! But the great advantage: At this point the audience is likely to be so tired they may not object to an age-old speaker's trick. The speaker, using some seemingly reasonable pretence, rejects the very formulation of the topic and then proceeds to talk about what he wanted to discuss in the first place, doing so precisely as he had wanted to make his comments. He simply decides what he thinks the Emperor's "nothing" is and how to present it.

DR. KLENBORT PRESENTS A THOUGHTFUL and searching discussion of Sullivan on the themes of self and individuality. She makes the important point that Sullivan's writings convey an ambiguity about individuality, as if present yet not accounted for. Thus, while Sullivan was committed to the exclusion of individuality, both from interpersonal theory and from the practice of psychiatry, he nevertheless makes reference to the unique in man, and does not hesitate to offer his own unique characterizations of man's difficulties in living. In pursuing the question of why Sullivan did not allow for the unique within his general theory Dr. Klenbort comes to the conclusion that, finally, he assigned overriding importance to adaptive (my italics) consensual validation.

I believe this is a telling and basic understanding. In essence, interpersonal theory concerns itself with the processes that underlie and generate one's adaptive or maladaptive adjustment to the interpersonal and cultural surround. In other words, the metatheory of interpersonal theory is that appropriate adaptation to the external world is valuable, indeed essential, in order to ensure social and psychological well-being. Sullivan put it this way at one point.

"It is necessary in the modification of activity in the interest of power in interpersonal relations—including … thought—that one focus, as it were, one's interest into certain fields that work. It is in learning this process that the self is evolved and the instrumentality of anxiety comes into being" (1947, p. 9).

Given this orientation, it is not surprising that Sullivan neglected those aspects of human nature (or, in other words, a conceptualization of human nature) that were not related to one's consensually validated standing in the environing culture. Whatever might be unique was simply useless or irrelevant to a psychiatry emphatically concerned with studying in operational terms, and promoting in operational terms, more effective social adjustment. More than this, the unique might be dangerous, or a sign of insanity insofar as it represented an autistic, non-consensual relationship with the culture.

To the Editor:

DR. IRENA KLENBORT'S PENETRATING paper, "Another Look at Sullivan's Concept of Individuality (This Journal, Volume 14, 1), is the latest in a series of efforts aimed at balancing out what has been regarded as the social adaptational bias in Interpersonal Theory—a bias which is out of place today, the "Age of the Self." It has been stated by Dr. Klenbort, and in some of the responding discussions by Drs. Crowley, Davis, Lefer and Lionells, that Sullivan was trying to ameliorate man's post-depression era and present technologically induced sense of isolation and insecurity. He therefore did not place his emphasis on man's uniqueness and originality, with their attendant dangers of grandiosity and alienation. In addition to this socio-economic reading of Sullivan's position, it should be noted (Davis touches on it) that Sullivan's position left scant room for the direct study of the unique, since what is unique cannot be operationally replicated. Yet, as Klenbort points out, why was it then that Sullivan was so attentive to the highly individualized in his clinical work, in addition to being such a unique person himself, while inveighing against what he considered to be that illusion of personal uniqueness in Interpersonal-Theory? It only adds to the mystery to note the numbers of analysts trained in his conceptions who went on to champion the importance of articulating the patient's uniqueness, in practice and theory.

In attempting to resolve this paradox, Dr. Klenbort and her respondents take a number of positions ranging from either the unique or the commonly connected, splitting the two, relegating one to practice and the other to theory, and the disclaiming of the existence of such a paradox to begin with.

ONE OF THE GREAT FAILINGS OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, particularly intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy (including psychoanalysis), is its inability to significantly alleviate the patient's suffering in a short period of time. Indeed, the prolongation of suffering has traditionally been extolled as a virtue on theoretical and technical grounds, and therapists have been warned that the premature cessation of suffering impedes therapeutic progress, thus making potentially greater gains impossible. The issue is less salient in brief or time-limited psychotherapy, the various forms of "supportive" psychotherapy, behavior modification, and other contemporary approaches that deviate from the classical psychoanalytic model, but the dictum has been tacitly accepted that the psychotherapist cannot expeditiously alleviate the patient's turmoil which frequently is the force propelling him in the direction of enlisting the help of a professional helper. to be sure, the trained psychotherapist has learned that he cannot work miracles, and that on many grounds he cannot meet the patient's magical expectations of rescue and help. Furthermore, it is obvious that the patient's current turmoil typically has a long history and that decades of maladaptive learning cannot be undone in a few sessions. However, if we are honest with ourselves, we are forced to admit that in the short run we are incapable of putting an end to the patient's suffering and discomfort; and that we cannot effectively stem the tide of the forces confronting us. In fact, it can be stated that there exists an inverse relationship between the ambitiousness of a psychotherapy and its ability to provide solace, psychoanalysis being in the forefront of the psychotherapies that make a virtue of suffering.

ANNA O. CALLED IT THE TALKING CURE and it would be most ungracious to censure her for not elaborating. Were one to elaborate in her place, one might add that if there is to be significant movement, let alone cure, a goodly amount of thinking would need to go along with the talking.

Thinking has not always been in good repute in psychoanalysis. Every now and then a certain ambiguity in the attitude toward thinking seems to surface. Thus thinking has at times been counterposed to feeling as if the two were incompatible or mutually exclusive. This may be a matter of how one understands thinking. I would like to suggest that thinking presupposes the ability to bear feeling and that it is an indispensable part of the psychoanalytic process.

In the course of daily work one notes a wide range of differences in how people approach and carry out the task of thinking. Some take to it as a duck takes to water; for others it remains for what seems forever an alien requirement, a kind of curiosity which they are surprised that anyone might expect them to engage in. The latter can, for instance, make the analyst feel that he or she must be mad to expect them to do this strange thing.

FACING THE EFFECTS WHICH different aspects of one's heritage have had on one's development is a necessary step in the process toward individuation and maturity. This process requires a person to deal with the totality of the life situation in which he grew up; not only his parents' socio-economic status, their ethnic cultural and religious background and their values, but also the parents' attitudes regarding themselves.

At first the influence of the parents is dominant, and psychoanalysis has, of course, explored this influence in many of its variations. The growth of the child is seen largely as a process of socialization and individuation. Thus the child is gradually prepared for assuming further responsibilities for himself as he enters the three- and four-year-old state, when, besides often helping younger children, he turns to explore the world and ask endless why's and what's. At the same time the seeming all-knowingness and all-powerfulness of the parents gradually begins to shrink.

One of the potentially richest periods of growth is adolescence. This is the time when the young man and woman should become able to deal consciously and deliberately with what has been presented to them as real and good. At this time, more than at any earlier time, young people should seek their won direction and orientation, choose a goal for their lives and a way to reach it.

PRACTICAL PROBLEMS FORCE THEMSELVES on us, and we have to look for answers to save our skins. Theoretical problems do not force themselves on us so directly. They are perennial, like problems of philosophy. As we age we develop a dignified modus vivendi in which we promise not to bother the problems and they in turn refrain from bothering us. It might even be that this insouciance is what distinguishes the mature therapist from the novice: the novice is a therapist who is aware of theoretical difficulties which make him uneasy and defensive. The mature therapist is no less comfortable than any workman with a difficult assignment. at worst he is defensive in response to his patient, but never in response to his calling. Unlike the novice, the veteran is stabilized by technical complacency.

If this seems a peculiar characterization, I remind you that one dominant way of training is to translate the trainee's work difficulties into terms of his own personal difficulties, and a logical implication of this is that there are no difficulties intrinsic to the work, i.e., no important theoretical problems of psychotherapy. I will pick this point up again later in connection with problems of training. I mention it here only as evidence that we may occasionally have to force-march ourselves into the theoretical wilderness to count and tag the puzzles that made trouble for us when we began and are still around even if they no longer trouble us.

Understanding vs. Attachment

Of these puzzles, I suppose, the one that we can most easily remember starting with is how to relate the effect of our spoken understandings to the effect of the developing personal relationship.

MY FIRST RESPONSE TO THE task of presenting a theory of the self was the realization that I have never formulated such a theory and

548

did not know if I had one. The task then became one of either discovering or creating it. Rather than simply presenting the outcome of my grapplings, I think it is more interesting to articulate the details of the process itself.

My search began, oddly enough, elsewhere. That is, I sampled the writings of some of the recognized "self" theorists, and concluded that there are different aspects of a theory of the self—the developmental, functional, structural, and pathological. For example, Laing (1965) writes primarily of the pathological modes of the self. Allport (1955) and Chein (1972) are concerned with the structure of the self. Freud and Sullivan deal with more than one aspect but from different viewpoints. In terms of development, Freud's main interest is in the libidinal or biological stages of development. Sullivan focuses on the interpersonal context in which the self system develops.

My intention in citing these examples is to indicate the unsettled nature of the field in attempting to come to grips with the concept of the self. Such terms as self, ego, person, self-system, self concept, self image, and self-identity are all in common usage, but all variously defined. It is difficult to know what aspects of a theory of self different writers are referring to, and even more difficult to know if they are using similar terms to mean similar things.

Brim (1975) has proposed that we think of the self as a theory we have about ourselves, thus adding the term self-theory to the above list. He claims that our self-theories are made up of inferences about ourselves based on observations of our own behavior and the reactions of others to us. This formulation highlighted for me what is a prevailing, yet frequently neglected, problem in the literature on the self, namely, the nature of the experienced "I". The experienced self is referred to variously as the core self, the self of selves, the knower of the other selves or the observing ego, but it rarely receives the attention that other aspects of a theory of the self do. Perhaps this is because it is so elusive. Some writers define the analysis of the experienced self as a philosophic rather than psychological problem, and leave it to the philosophers to deal with. However, that is precisely the aspect of a theory of the self that most interests me, what might be called the phenomenological aspect.

DURING THE PAST SEVERAL YEARS I have been engaged in the process of treating deeply disturbed, hospitalized patients with long-term intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy. In reviewing my work, as well as the reports of colleagues, I have found increasing confirmation for the idea that significant change in a patient's understanding of himself and his world is inextricably bound to a parallel process of questioning and growth on the part of the therapist. The formation of an intense therapeutic relationship with a very troubled individual necessarily leads the therapist to a painful questioning of his traditional theoretical posture and accepted technical procedure, often ultimately stimulating considerable uncertainty with regard to aspects of his professional and personal identity. This paper provides an account of the first year of treatment with a young woman hospitalized with the diagnosis of "schizophrenic character disorder." The clinical material presented here illustrates how one therapist's effort to engage in radical inquiry into, and modification of, his own theory, technique and personal response in the clinical situation facilitated subsequent inquiry and similar efforts at integration by the patient.

During the course of this therapeutic endeavor, I participated in a study group which considered in detail some aspects of the work of Jacques Lacan. In the midst of mounting confusion with regard to the patient and her psychotherapy, my discovery of Lacan was a serendipitous event, providing a fresh conceptual framework and personal stimulus for modifying the understanding of this patient's difficulties, making possible a reorientation of practice. THIS PAPER IS ONE OF A SERIES of studies, essentially personal, which have grown out of and are therefore an extension of the investigation of the nature of the psychoanalyic process which I reported in my book (1967). In that work I left rather empty the description of the interpretive function of the analyst as one of his modes of participation in the therapeutic relationship, since it was not central to the main theme. This centered on the process and its evolution seen as arising essentially in the unconscious of the patient. But it is probably true that any analysis which really taps the passions of the patient does the same for the analyst and promotes a development which can further his own self-analysis. Insofar as this is true, the main industrial hazard of this work lies in the danger of the transference-countertransference process taking a turn in the direction of perversion and thus becoming anti-therapeutic for both members of the undertaking.

The analyst's great safeguard against this lies in the method and its basic technique, any breach of which should serve as a warning bell that the countertransference requires special scrutiny.

I

Psychoanalysis: Cure or Persuasion?

"WHEN (PSYCHOANALYSIS) BECOMES AN institution, when it is applied to so-called 'normal subjects, ' it utterly ceases to be a conception that can be justified or discussed on the basis of cases: it no longer cures, it persuades; it shapes for itself subjects who conform to its own interpretation of man. It has its converts and perhaps its rebels; it can no longer convince. Beyond the true and the false, it is a myth, and Freudianism thus degraded is no longer an interpretation, but a variant of the Oedipus Myth." (Lévi-Strauss, 1963)

My most consistent interest has been the perplexing relationship between what the psychoanalyst formulates about what he does and what he actually does in therapy (Levenson, 1972). And, if the process of therapy does not follow straightforwardly, as I suspect it does not, from the theory, how does the therapist know how to do what he does, when he does it? Certainly it must be agreed that therapists of different persuasions all get results they deem satisfactory. Are they doing different things, or the same thing in different ways? Are there different cures? If the treatment depends on the metapsychology of the therapist, is it not just an ideological conversion? Then, what one therapist calls "cure" is nothing more than a successful proselytization, i.e., the patient is now fine according to the therapist's scriptures.

This gap between practice and theory exists in any activity that can be performed and described. It is equally true of art, dance or skiing. In most activities, though, the theory is understood to be no more than a temporary manual of procedure on which to lean until the process becomes automatic. Theory, in these instances, may not

WE THINK OF PSYCHOANALYSIS AS AN exploration of the mind of the analysand, a search in which we find in him ideas, emotions, motives, which have been there all along but of which he had been heretofore unaware. Introduction

AS A PSYCHOANALYST ACCRUES EXPERIENCE as a therapist and teacher, he comes to recognize that his basic commitment to the clinical psychoanalytic and psychotherapeutic situations carries with it a number of peripheral, albeit important, areas of interest and even concern. Thus, in addition to his basic responsibilities to his patients, the psychoanalyst may find himself embroiled in debates and constructive efforts in such areas as the social impact of emotional illness and the broader problem of the psychological dimensions of culture and society; the narrower field of the political and organizational structure of psychoanalysis itself, and of communication among psychoanalysts; the basic clinical methodology of the psychoanalytic therapist and researcher; and a host of comparable problems. This kind of widening scope of the analyst's activities confronts him with situations in which his basic clinical methodology and expertise cannot guide or fulfill either his own needs or those with whom he deals on these "alien" grounds. He must then both face his limitations as a clinician in an unfamiliar field, and search for new and more appropriate guides and insights if he is to contribute meaningfully in these broader areas.

My own preference has been to work within the clinical psychoanalytic and psychotherapeutic situations, and to endeavor to broaden my understanding of this special, bipersonal field.

I WISH TO DISCUSS MY MISGIVINGS about the construct of countertransference as originally formulated and then to examine how my thoughts have evolved in respect to this problem.

The classical formulation troubled me because I accepted the validity of the need to correct unconstructive intrusions by the therapist into the therapeutic transaction but also intuited that the correction could lead to an impoverishment of therapeutic experience. While not certain that this challenge would be construed as valid to others, I believed an unacknowledged scientific controversy was emerging. I expressed myself on this topic in an article entitled "Exploring the Therapeutic Use of Countertransference Data" (Tauber, 1954). The issues as I saw them then, are expressed in the introductory passage of this article:

This paper is designed to illustrate the fact that countertransference phenomena may under certain circumstances afford an opportunity to evoke new material about the patient, the analyst, or the relationship, and that they may be used therapeutically to increase mutual spontaneity. The author believes that there is a real need for developing a scientific method to utilize constructively the negative components introduced by the therapist in the treatment situation and to determine which of these components are worthy of mutual exploration. According to classical psychoanalytic theory, countertransference reactions represent unanalyzed portions of the therapist's personality which either transparently or unwittingly interfere with the treatment situation. These reactions may be due to blind spots, private needs, irrelevant attitudes, biases, or moral prejudices; and they call for a change to a more productive orientation, necessitating their analysis. This is the basis in psychoanalytic theory for recognizing that any person engaged in intensive psychotherapeutic work with others needs a training analysis—a recognition which represents one of the most valuable discoveries in psychoanalysis.

THOMAS CARLYLE, WRITING ON HISTORY, asked, "What is knowledge … but recorded experience, and a product of history; of which, therefore, reasoning and belief, no less than action and passion, are essential materials?" This admonition might well be directed to modern psychoanalysts struggling with the concept of insight and its relationship to therapeutic change. I will suggest in this paper that a shift of emphasis is necessary for our concept of insight to become a more effective tool in the goals of therapy. To be effective for change and growth, insight must include clarification and repair of disordered cognition, the individual's ways of knowing both sensate and syntactic experience.

When we consider that psychoanalytic theories have in common assumptions that much of human behavior and mental functioning stem from unconscious processes, from needs, thoughts, feelings, actions and premises about living that lie outside of awareness, a concept of insight is inevitable. Yet different theories emphasize the importance of different insights and often use different explanatory systems for organizing them. With time, both the development of our theories and our experience with patients have also expanded the base of significant knowledge that becomes important in understanding the complexities of people's difficulties in living. Indeed, our concepts of insight have become so diffuse and expanded, that a sense of futility and frustration often attends our attempts to encompass all into the design of effective insight therapies.

SULLIVAN CREDITED THREE GREAT therapists with significantly influencing his thinking in psychiatry, Sigmund Freud, Adolf Meyer, and William A. White. From each, he acquired certain aspects of his approach to the problems of mental illness. From Freud, he obtained many fundamental orientations. Through Meyer, he was influenced in his thinking of mental illness as a dynamic pattern of behavior, as a way of reacting to life, and from White, he acquired some of the practical aspects of his therapeutic approach. Meyer and White directly influenced his life through personal contact and teaching. Sullivan never met Freud but he was an earnest student of his writings.

He entered the field of psychiatry around 1920. Unlike Freud, his first contacts were with psychotic patients. He only later became orders. For many years, he devoted his research to an attempt to apply psychoanalytic theory and technique to the therapy of the psychotic. Jung and Bleuler before him had found psychoanalytic theory useful in explaining some of the behavior and symbolization of the psychotic, but psychoanalysis as a method of therapy for the psychotic had hardly begun. In fact, it was considered dangerous and is still so considered to treat the psychotic by the classical Freudian methods. It was believed that classical analysis could precipitate psychosis in a borderline case and that therefore all attempts at psychoanalyzing psychotics should be avoided. At the same time, much of Freud's thinking was creeping into the orientation of psychiatrists in America. The importance of the experiences of early childhood in producing later difficulties was being stressed. Another Look at Sullivan's Concept of Individuality

Irena Klenbort Ph.D.

Irena Klenbort

Irena Klenbort, Ph.D.
50 West 67 Street
New York, New York 10023

Irena Klenbort  

THE CAREFUL READER CANNOT escape a sense of an intellectual ambivalence in Sullivan's writings, a disturbing ambiguity concerning the themes of self and individuality. Certainly he writes, "We are all more simply human than otherwise, " and in order to be so we are all more alike than otherwise, indeed without uniqueness. Self-generated individuality is an illusion, to Sullivan, and we are each the sum of the reflected appraisals of others. Yet at the same time, it is Sullivan who is able to capture and describe psychological types, or syndromes as he calls them, whose various personalities and pathologies have a vivid and idiosyncratic quality usually expected from a novelist rather than a doctor. These syndromes describe people who are indeed more human than otherwise. And in many respects they have more individuality than those described by the usual psychoanalytic diagnostic categories.

There is, therefore, a paradox at the center of Sullivan's theory of human nature and psychotherapy which lurks in much of his work and can make reading his lectures a puzzling experience. This paradox has been delineated clearly in a paper by Crowley (1973).

Crowley indicates Sullivan rejected that concept of unique individuality which was distorted and neurotic but not that one which was real; this latter Sullivan saw as being beyond the possibility of consensual observation and therefore out of the reach of a scientific psychiatry. Crowley points out that there is no denial of personal individuality as such and so the issue becomes one of definition and methodology. Summarizing Sullivan, he writes:

In theory, individuality is liquidated; in practice, it becomes a goal, in the sense of responding to the real characteristics of another person. A paradox indeed! A Perspective on Responsibility

Edgar Levenson M.D.

Edgar Levenson

Edgar A. Levenson, M.D.
125 East 87th Street
New York, New York 10028

Edgar Levenson  

TO BEGIN WITH, THE "SELF" is not a topology of mind like ego, id and superego, but a perspective on awareness and an interpersonal one, at that. The self is the way an individual personifies himself as he stands outside of himself. It is an act of hallucinatory self-consciousness. The exact nature of self and how it develops is a Pandora's box of reflected appraisals, introjects, projects and hallucinatory percepts. As M. Khan (1974) puts it,

… no matter how zealously or critically one studies this varied and perplexing literature, no clear definition of self, as a concept, crystallizes; although each of us feels sure about what he means when he uses the concept self, it is hard to communicate the meaning to another … no one can communicate directly from his self or can be related to directly in his self.

I intend to limit myself to the implications of this for therapy. There would hardly be any point in having a symposium on our differences in the theory of self unless it were an a priori assumption that one's theory of self affects the way one does therapy. Therefore, I suspect that we are really talking indirectly about our theories of responsibility and change in psychoanalytic therapy. For example, if we were to believe that man is predetermined, condemned by original sin, socio-economic and cultural oppression, biological and biochemical deficiency or even very early deprivation, it would clearly affect our attitude about what could be done to ameliorate the patient's circumstances and how best to go about it. It seems to me that there is a continuum of perspectives on responsibility (or freedom)

W. W. Norton & Co., Inc., New York, N.Y. 1977

DR. DAHLBERG IS A PSYCHOANALYST who likes to write books about the obvious. What is the obvious, particularly for an analyst, and what does it conceal? A prior book by the senior author: "From Food to Fertilizer—the Role of Excrement in the Life Cycle" (Young, Scott Books, Reading, Mass., 1973) is an earlier effort in the direction of recognizing and appreciating what lies behind the obvious.

The present volume, expertly co-authored by Dr. Joseph Jaffe, familiarizes us with a significant and wide-spread cause of morbidity and mortality—namely, cerebro-vascular disease. The focus is on left hemispheric lesions leading to aphasia. It is pointed out that on the basis of hospital admissions, "five to six hundred thousand people in the United States suffer a stroke each year, and a majority do survive. Two-and-a-half-million stroke victims are alive in America today." We also are reminded that because the incidence of survival is high, stroke becomes the most costly disease in this country.

The authors have selected to write about aphasia because of their special interest in communication. Thus, in addition to providing us with an interesting personal account of Dr. Dahlberg's neurological syndrome, an extremely lucid and illuminating section on linguistics is included. As all of us must acknowledge, the language function distinguishes us from the rest of the animal kingdom—it defines a unique property of man.

IT IS THE BASIC PURPOSE of this paper1. to outline, discuss, and synthesize a series of clinical postulates regarding countertransference, developed through an adaptational-interactional approach to this dimension of therapeutic and analytic relationships. These postulates are based on an amalgam of clinical observations and an extensive review of the psychoanalytic literature (Langs, 1976a), (1976b), and they will shaped with a view toward enhancing our understanding of the treatment interaction and with some stress on their pertinence to analytic and therapeutic technique1. The present investigation of countertransference is somewhat different than the prior explorations that I have undertaken (Langs, 1974), (1976a), (1976b), in that I shall focus almost exclusively on the interactional aspects of countertransference and shall concentrate on recent conceptions developed largely since those earlier publications—some of which have not been considered at all in the prior writings of myself or others.

Introduction

THE BURGEONING LITERATURE ON countertransference includes several reviews (Glover, 1955) ; (Orr, 1954) ; (Reich, 1960), the most recent and comprehensive of which is that of Langs (1976), although it restricts itself to writings which are available in English. As is consonant with the earlier view that psychoanalytic therapy is applicable only to neurotics, the vast majority of relevant material pertains to their treatment.

Freud (1910) introduced the term countertransference a few years before he wrote the bulk of his papers on technique, although he never devoted a special study to it. It was considered roughly as the obverse of transference, the repetition of the analyst's irrational, previously acquired attitudes, now directed toward the patient, and was assumed to be absent except in situations in which the therapist was inadequately analyzed. Freud deemed it to be the obligation of the analyst to eliminate such unconscious reactions as obstacles to treatment. Earlier, he had described how Breuer reacted to Anna O's erotic transference with anxiety and took a hurried vacation with his wife (Breuer and Freud, 1893-1895).

Today the definition of countertransference remains unsettled. Most analysts see Freud's original use of the term to define countertransference neuroses. Many, in agreement with Alexander (1948) and Little (1957), view countertransference to consist of all of the therapist's emotional responses to the patient but perhaps more see it as representing the whole of the analyst's unconscious reactions to the individual analyzand and particularly to the analyzand's own transference. "IT IS NOT SURPRISING THAT psycho-analysis confirms our recognition of the important place which folk fairy tales have acquired in the mental life of our children" (Freud, 1913, p. 281). In their timelessness, lack of ambiguity, vivid imagery, symbolism, and endorsement of magic, fairy tales are compatible with the primary process thought of early life. In The Uses of Enchantment, the first comprehensive psychoanalytic interpretation of fairy tales, Bruno Bettelheim (1976) illuminates the congruence between structural aspects of fairy tales and the child's psyche. He vigorously argues that this form of literature, above all others, facilitates the growth of the ego and has therapeutic value for each child.

Distinguishing the fairy tale from myths, fables, and realistic stories, Bettelheim explains that only fairy tales speak of everyday characters who confront crucial existential problems and emerge unscathed and joyful. A true fairy tale, in Bettelheim's view, must have a happy ending. We propose, in contrast to Bettelheim, that fairy tales frequently do not present the child with a view of the world which helps him expand his knowledge of human beings or modify his perception of right and wrong. II General Systems Theory: Model or Muddle

Edgar Levenson M.D.

Edgar Levenson

Edgar A. Levenson, M.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, New York 10023

Edgar Levenson  

GENERAL SYSTEMS THEORY IS A DOCTRINE of genuine theoretical and practical merit. By virtue of its being a 'theory of theories' it profers a twofold vantage to psychotherapists; first, it brings psychotherapy into a systematic relationship with other sciences, not just social sciences, and second, it offers a specific model, metaphor, or if you prefer 'paradigm' for conceptualizing the process of therapy. Its somewhat immodest promise is that of the philosopher's stone; a theory that explains everything and shows the inherent connection and transformational calculus of everything. Yet, this heady brew has lead to more intoxication than solid results. As has been the fate of many doctrines in their passage from the mouths of the innovators to the hands of the acolytes, it has undergone lip service, banalization, cooptation and downright misunderstanding. "Homeostasis", "open system", "closed loop", "feedback" are used in a fashion that is more modish than original. Often, the underlying theoretical paradigm seems more related to W.B. Cannon's physiological homeostatis or Kurt Lewin's field theory: both admirable concepts, but neither entirely current, and certainly not general systems theory.

To be both vital and relevant, a new model must meet several criteria. First, it must offer a coherent model for phenomena not completely or adequately subsumed under the old model. That is, the accumulated discordant data precede the theory and the theory emerges under the pressure of the need for a new explanatory system. If this is not so, then one is simply fitting a new terminology to old data and the rule of parsimony applies, the new theory is simply superfluous. Second, the theory must re-organize the way its practitioners perceive the data, so that new data emerge or the old data shift their emphases. Third, the new model must have a certain aesthetic harmoniousness for the theorist. Kuhn has said that scientific paradigms change when the old theorists die or fade away (Kuhn, 1962). The implication then is that changing one's model of scientific inquiry is not entirely a volitional process. One is more or less stuck with one's own time and place and style.

Sullivan's Concept of Malevolent Transformation (A Symposium)—Malevolent Transformation and the Negative Therapeutic Reaction

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
250 East 87th Street
New York, New York 10028

Gerard Chrzanowski  

MALEVOLENT TRANSFORMATION is an interpersonal term coined by Harry Stack Sullivan (1953). It refers to a compulsive display of hostility when a need for tenderness arises. The phenomenon of malevolent transformation reflects a pattern of biting the hand that one would like to be stroked by tenderly.

Dynamically malevolent transformation is the outgrowth of a developmental miscarriage. The core of the malevolent personality warp, according to Sullivan, is the consistent experience of expecting rebuff and humiliation whenever a need for tenderness, for friendly cooperation is displayed. As a protective or defensive counterreaction, people with these experiences act hatefully when they feel a need for tenderness. The anticipatory malevolence is further aided by the intervention of selective inattention i.e., a consistent pattern of looking "the other way "when an actual friendly response occurs. Selective inattention hinders a beginning discriminatory attitude that would enable the person to be more discerning between an accepting or rejecting interpersonal atmosphere.

Sullivan was of the opinion that malevolent transformation is "perhaps the greatest disaster that happens in the childhood phase of personality development" (Sullivan, 1953, p. 216)

M. Fromm Ph.D.

M. Fromm

M. Gerard Fromm, Ph.D.

M. Fromm  

THE PROPOSITION THAT I WISH to present in this paper evolves rather logically from the growing body of analytic work with severely disturbed patients, and from the reflections about the nature of the therapy process which this has stimulated. There is now, within the analytic community, a durable consensus about the following basic ideas:

1. the therapist, especially with borderline and psychotic patients, constantly brings his developmental knowledge and technical sensibility to bear on the intensity and even the kinds of transference phenomena in a given treatment; (Kernberg, 1975) ; (Kohut, 1971) ; (Ramzy, 1961) ; (Searles, 1961a), (1961b)

2. the therapist utilizes constructively (that is, apprehends, modulates, analyzes, and in some way informs the treatment about) his countertransference reactions to the patient; (Greenson, 1974) ; (Kernberg, 1975) ; (Feiner, 1977 and many others), even as,

3. the patient unconsciously needs to stimulate countertransference reactions in the therapist—for purposes including defense, the communication of preverbal or preconceptual experience, of a real or fantasied nature, (Khan, 1963, and others) ; or the integration within the therapist-parent of that which the original parent had to dissociate (Searles, 1959), (1961b).

This paper extends this train of thought slightly, and humbly addresses subtle degrees of countertransference and the necessary preliminaries to an analytic focus on them. It is my hypothesis that the patient notices increments of countertransference feeling, frequently prior to the therapist reaching this awareness; and in one way or another reflects this back to the therapist.
